analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting health coverage for workers on strike or locked out.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 Democratic and independent senators, was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can cut off an employee's health insurance while that employee is on a lawful strike or while the employer is locking out workers to pressure them in contract negotiations. This bill would make that an illegal unfair labor practice, with civil penalties up to $75,000 per violation for lockouts and $50,000 for strikes, doubled for repeat violators, and it would let regulators hold individual directors and officers liable for violations. It would not require employers to keep paying premiums for workers who stop working during a strike if the union contract says otherwise; it addresses only the termination or alteration of the coverage itself.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on strike or locked out, and their families, who today can lose employer health coverage precisely when they have no paycheck — often mid-treatment or mid-pregnancy. Unions would also gain negotiating leverage: employers could no longer use the threat of losing health insurance to force contract concessions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Striking and locked-out workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act to make it illegal for an employer to terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage during a lockout or during a lawful strike. [S3]

It sets civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for coverage cuts during a lockout and $50,000 during a lawful strike, doubled to $150,000 or $100,000 respectively when the violation coincides with a discharge or serious economic harm and the employer violated the same rule within the past five years. [S3]

It allows the National Labor Relations Board to assess penalties directly against a director or officer who directed or committed the violation, or who knew of it and had the authority to prevent it but failed to. [S3]
The Board would weigh the gravity of the employer's actions, the employer's size, its history of violations, and the public interest in setting penalty amounts. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers with unionized workforces, especially in industries with frequent strikes and lockouts, which would continue bearing health coverage costs during labor disputes and face new federal penalties for cutting coverage. Health insurers would keep receiving premiums during strikes that today often end.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new costs on employers during strikes and lockouts: continuing coverage for workers who are not working raises the expense of labor disputes and could make employers more reluctant to lock out workers or could harden bargaining positions. [S3]
It changes bargaining dynamics by removing health coverage as a lever employers can use to press for contract terms, which some would argue tilts collective bargaining further toward unions. [S3]
The bill only prohibits terminating or altering coverage; it does not resolve who pays premiums during a strike, so its practical protection depends on existing plan terms and union contracts. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and falls on a narrow but vulnerable group: workers who lose both income and health coverage at the same moment, sometimes mid-treatment. The cost falls on employers with unionized workforces, for whom continued coverage during strikes is a real but bounded expense. The bill's protection is not absolute — it preserves rather than mandates coverage — so its value depends on the underlying plan. The main weakness is political: it never moved, so the weighing never got a public test.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 8, 2023, joined by 12 Democratic and independent senators including Casey, Sanders, Warren, Fetterman, Durbin, and Baldwin. [S3] [S4]
All 12 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or independents; no Republican cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction — the only action it ever received. [S5]
The committee took no further action, and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with unionized workforces are better off, because they retain the ability to terminate or alter health coverage during strikes and lockouts without facing the bill's civil penalties. Striking and locked-out workers remain exposed to losing coverage during labor disputes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who cut coverage during strikes

industries.note: The bill would require these employers to keep health coverage intact during strikes and lockouts and expose them to civil penalties up to $75,000 per violation, doubled for repeat violators, plus possible director and officer liability. Its purpose is to remove health coverage as a pressure tactic in labor disputes, which is why employers' interest runs against the workers it protects.

Insurers would keep collecting premiums for striking and locked-out workers who today often lose coverage, but they would also face continued coverage of members during disputes with little change to their operations. The effect on them is secondary to the bill's target, employers.
